title: Development of Lorentz Four-dimensional Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy for Quantitative Measurements of in-situ Current-driven Magnetic Domain Wall Deformations
content: Four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) allows for quantitative measurements of a sample’s differential phase transmission function and has led to a recent surge of interest in atomic resolution mapping of strain, electric and magnetic fields within materials critical to human infrastructure and computing [1]. Field-free or Lorentz electron microscopy with a variable applied field is necessary for studying magnetic materials in detail such as mapping their magnetic phase diagram or measuring current-driven spin texture dynamics [2,3]. In conventional STEM geometries, Lorentz mode is achieved by turning the objective lens off and variable fields via small applied excitations of the objective lens. However, this leads to large thermal fluctuations in the TEM column and noticeable drift upon returning to high-resolution mode which takes ten or more hours to diminish [4].
